p: The letter opens the way John's Gospel does, with "beginning", but it does not say which beginning.
b: The Gospel of John opens, "In the beginning was the Word" (John 1:1), echoing Genesis 1:1. This letter says ap' archēs, "from the beginning". Two readings: (1) the beginning of all things, so that "what was from the beginning" is the eternal life that "was with the Father" (1:2); (2) the beginning of the good news, when Jesus came and the first disciples heard him, which is what "from the beginning" means later in the letter (2:7, 24; 3:11). Many readers think the writer means both at once. The Plain keeps "from the beginning" in every place, so the reader can follow the word; the Gospel's Plain renders the same Greek "from the start" at John 8:44 and John 15:27.

p: The "we" of the opening may be eyewitnesses of Jesus, or the community that keeps their witness.
b: The letter begins with "we" and only later says "I" (2:1). Readers take the "we" three ways. (1) Eyewitnesses: the writer speaks for those who saw Jesus, as the church traditionally held of the apostle John. (2) The community: "we" are the keepers of the eyewitness tradition, a circle of teachers who speak for it against those who left (2:19). (3) A teacher's "we" of authority, the way a leader speaks for his church. The senses are concrete (heard, seen with our eyes, gazed at, touched), which suits the first or second view. The same "we" closes John's Gospel: "And we know his testimony is true" (John 21:24).

p: Touch was the proof that Jesus had a real body, the point the opponents denied (4:2).
b: The verb psēlaphaō means to feel with the hands, the word the risen Jesus uses in Luke: "Feel me and look: a spirit has no flesh and bones, and you can see that I have them" (Luke 24:39). Hearing and seeing could be claimed for a vision; touching could not. The letter will say that the test of a true spirit is to confess "Jesus Christ as having come in the flesh" (4:2), so the opening sets out the evidence at once. Early readers used the verse this way: Tertullian quotes it, "That, says John, which we have seen with our eyes, which we have looked upon, and our hands have handled, of the Word of life" (Against Praxeas 15).

t: "The word of life": a person or a message?
p: Logos can mean the Word, Jesus himself (John 1:1), or the message that brings life.
b: The Greek peri tou logou tēs zōēs can be read (1) as the Word who is life, Jesus, as in "the Word became flesh" (John 1:14), since what was "touched" must be a person; or (2) as the message about life, as in Paul's "holding out the word of life" (Philippians 2:16); or (3) both: the message that is about, and is, the living Christ. The pronouns before it are neuter ("what"), not "who", which leans toward the message; the next verse speaks of "the life" made visible, which leans toward the person. The Plain keeps a lower-case "word" so that every reading stays open. Verse 1:1 has no main verb of its own: its "what" clauses are picked up by "we announce" in 1:3, after the aside of 1:2. The Plain supplies "this is what we speak of" from peri, "about", so that 1:1 can stand as a sentence.
orig: περὶ τοῦ λόγου τῆς ζωῆς (peri tou logou tēs zōēs)

p: Phaneroō, "make visible, reveal", comes nine times in this short letter.
b: The verb phaneroō means to bring into the open what was hidden. 1 John uses it nine times: of the life that was with the Father (1:2, twice), of those who left (2:19), of Christ's coming again (2:28; 3:2), of what believers will be (3:2), of his first coming (3:5, 8) and of God's love (4:9). The Plain says "made visible" or "appeared" so the reader can hear that one word ties together Jesus' first coming and his return. John's Gospel says that in the Word was life, "and the life was humanity's light" (John 1:4).

a: the eternal life that was with the Father
p: The phrase echoes "the Word was with God" (John 1:1) and calls Jesus himself "the eternal life".
b: "Eternal life" (zōē aiōnios) is literally "the life of the age", the life of the age to come. Here it is not only something believers receive (2:25; 5:11) but someone who "was with the Father" (pros ton patera) and "was made visible to us": the Gospel's "the Word was with God" (pros ton theon, John 1:1) in other words. The letter ends the same way, calling the Son "the real God and eternal life" (5:20). John's Gospel defines it: "Eternal life is this: to know you, the only real God, and the one you sent, Jesus Christ" (John 17:3).

p: Koinōnia means having something in common: a shared life, a partnership.
b: Koinōnia comes from koinos, "common, shared". It was used of business partners, of marriage, of friends who share everything. Paul uses it for the Philippians' "partnership in the good news" (Philippians 1:5). Here it has two sides that cannot be pulled apart: sharing life with the eyewitness "we", and sharing life "with the Father, and with his Son". To leave the community, as some had (2:19), was in the writer's view to leave the fellowship with God that it carries. The word comes four times in 1:3-7 and nowhere else in John's writings.

p: Christos is Greek for the Hebrew mashiach, "anointed one". In this letter it is never just a name.
b: Christos translates the Hebrew mashiach, "anointed", the title of Israel's kings and of the king to come. In the letters the site writes "Christ" as part of Jesus' name, and "the Messiah" where the claim itself is at stake (2:22; 5:1). In 1 John the word keeps its meaning. Its readers have an "anointing" (chrisma, 2:20, 27); the enemies of the truth are "antichrists" (2:18); and the liar is the one who denies that Jesus is the Christ, the Anointed One (2:22).

p: The words are Jesus' own at the Last Supper in John's Gospel, and they return at the end of 2 John.
b: "So that your joy will be filled up" is Jesus' promise in the Gospel (John 16:24), with the same Greek, hina hē chara ... ē peplērōmenē, and he prays that his disciples will have his joy "filled to the full" (John 17:13). The letter turns the Lord's words around: the writers' joy will be full when the readers share their fellowship. 2 John 12 ends with the same phrase. On "our" and "your" joy, see the variant.

p: One of three short sayings about God in John's writings: God is spirit, God is light, God is love.
b: John's writings have three sentences of the form "God is ...": "God is spirit" (John 4:24), "God is light" (here) and "God is love" (4:8, 16). Light here is not a substance but a picture of goodness and truth: in God there is nothing hidden, false or evil, "not the least bit". The Old Testament has the same picture (Psalm 27:1; Isaiah 60:19-20), and in John's Gospel Jesus says, "I am the light of the world" (John 8:12). The next verses draw the lesson: those who claim to share life with God must walk in the light.
r: John 4:24; 4:8, 16; Psalm 27:1; Isaiah 60:19-20; John 1:4-9; John 8:12; James 1:17

p: The Dead Sea Scrolls also divide people into children of light and of darkness, ruled by two spirits.
b: The Community Rule (1QS), found at Qumran by the Dead Sea, teaches that God set two spirits over humanity. In Geza Vermes's translation: "Those born of truth spring from a fountain of light, but those born of falsehood spring from a source of darkness"; the children of righteousness are ruled "by the Prince of Light", and "all the children of falsehood are ruled by the Angel of Darkness" (Community Rule, column 3, lines 19-21). 1 John shares the pairs: light and darkness, truth and lie, "the Spirit of truth and the spirit that leads astray" (4:6). Most scholars see a shared Jewish way of speaking rather than borrowing. A difference: in 1QS the line is drawn by God's plan; in 1 John it shows in how people walk and love.

a: If we say we have fellowship
p: Three "if we say" lines (1:6, 8, 10) may quote what the writer's opponents were saying.
b: The letter tests three claims, each with "if we say": fellowship with God while walking in darkness (1:6); having no sin (1:8); never having sinned (1:10). Three "the one who says" lines follow (2:4, 6, 9). Some read them as the slogans of those who had left (2:19), people who claimed to know God and to be beyond sin. Others think they are general warnings that any believer could fall into, since the writer says "we". The answer to each claim is not argument but a test of life: walking, confessing, keeping commands, loving.

p: In John, truth is not only something you believe but something you do.
b: "To practice the truth" (poiein tēn alētheian) is a Hebrew way of speaking: to "do truth" is to act faithfully. The Gospel uses it: "But the one who practices the truth comes to the light, so that his works may be shown to have been done in God" (John 3:21). Truth in this letter is a way of living as much as a set of facts: a liar is someone whose life contradicts his claim (2:4), and love must be a matter "of deeds and of truth" (3:18).
orig: οὐ ποιοῦμεν τὴν ἀλήθειαν (ou poioumen tēn alētheian)

t: "Walk": a Jewish word for a way of life
p: To "walk" is the Bible's picture for how one lives; Jewish law is called halakhah, "the walking".
b: "Walk" (peripateō, Hebrew halakh) is the Bible's everyday picture for conduct: Enoch "walked with God", and Israel is to walk in the LORD's ways. Rabbinic Judaism calls its practical law halakhah, from the same Hebrew root: the way one walks. 1 John uses the word five times (1:6, 7; 2:6 twice; 2:11). To walk in the light is not to have a feeling but to live openly, honestly and in love, in step with the way Jesus walked (2:6).

a: makes us clean from every sin
p: The language is the Day of Atonement's: atonement that makes the people clean from all their sins.
b: "Make clean" (katharizō) is the Torah's word for purification. On the Day of Atonement Moses is told, "For on this day atonement will be made for you, to make you clean. You will be clean from all your sins before the LORD" (Leviticus 16:30). The letter says the same of "the blood of Jesus his Son", meaning his death, and says it in the present tense: it goes on making clean those who walk in the light. The next verses show that this is not for the sinless but for those who confess (1:9). See also "the atoning sacrifice" (2:2).

p: Whoever claims to be without sin leads himself astray. This sits in tension with 3:6-9.
b: The claim may have come from the opponents, who perhaps held that the spiritual person was beyond sin, or it may be a warning to the faithful. Calvin, commenting on the verse, notes that Augustine used it against the Pelagians, who held that a person could live without sin. The Catholic Catechism quotes 1:8-9 together in its teaching on mercy and sin (paragraph 1847). John Wesley read the verse through 1:10: "the tenth verse fixes the sense of the eighth", so the point is that all have sinned, not that a believer must go on sinning (Sermon 40, Christian Perfection, II.19). The letter will also say that the one born from God "does not sin" (3:6, 9): see the note and the deep dive there.

p: To confess is to say the same thing about one's sins that God says. The verse does not say to whom.
b: Homologeō means "say the same": agree, admit openly. Israel confessed sin aloud: the high priest confessed "all the guilty deeds and rebellions of the Israelites, all their sins" over the goat (Leviticus 16:21), and the psalmist said, "I will confess my rebellious acts to the LORD" (Psalm 32:5). Calvin used this verse to argue that confession is owed to God, since "it is the Lord who forgives" (Institutes 3.4.9). The Catholic and Orthodox practice of confession to a priest rests mainly on John 20:23 and James 5:16, not on this verse; the Council of Trent's chapter on confession (session 14, chapter 5) does not cite it. See the card at John 20:23.

a: he is faithful and he is just
p: One expects mercy to forgive, not justice. The letter says God's justice forgives too.
b: "Faithful" (pistos) recalls God's covenant character, "great in loyal love and faithfulness" (Exodus 34:6): he keeps his promise to forgive. "Just" (dikaios) is harder. Readers explain it three ways: (1) God is just to forgive because the sin has been dealt with, by "the blood of Jesus" (1:7) and the "atoning sacrifice" (2:2); (2) in Hebrew thought God's righteousness is his saving faithfulness to his people, so "just" and "faithful" say nearly the same thing; (3) God is true to his own word, which promises mercy to those who confess (Proverbs 28:13).
orig: πιστός ἐστιν καὶ δίκαιος (pistos estin kai dikaios)

a: we are making him a liar
p: "Liar" is one of the letter's sharpest words: it comes five times.
b: To say "we have not sinned" contradicts God, who says that we have, so it makes him out to be a liar. The word pseustēs comes five times in 1 John: the one who claims to know God but disobeys (2:4), the one who denies that Jesus is the Messiah (2:22), the one who says he loves God but hates his brother (4:20), and the one who does not believe God's testimony, who "has made him a liar" (5:10). In John's Gospel the devil is "a liar and the father of falsehood" (John 8:44).

p: Teknia, a word of affection, is how Jesus addresses his disciples at the Last Supper.
b: The writer now says "I" for the first time and calls his readers teknia, "little children", a fond diminutive. Jesus uses it once in the Gospels, to the disciples at the Last Supper: "Little children, I will be with you just a short while more" (John 13:33). 1 John uses it six times in NA28, which the Plain follows (seven in editions that also read it at 3:7), and also paidia, "children" (2:13, 18; and 3:7 in NA28). It is the voice of an old teacher to people he regards as his own, which fits the tradition of an aged John at Ephesus, and also fits a respected elder of any age.

p: Paraklētos, a person called to stand beside you, is the Spirit in John's Gospel and Jesus here.
b: In the Gospel Jesus says, "I will request it of the Father, and he will give you another Advocate to be with you for all time" (John 14:16): the Spirit is "another" Advocate, which implies that Jesus is the first. Here Jesus is the Advocate "with the Father", pleading for those who sin, as the high priest does in Hebrews 7:25. The word paraklētos means one called to someone's side, especially in court; English Bibles have "advocate", "helper", "comforter" and "counselor". The site uses "Advocate" in every place, so the reader can see that it is one word.

p: Dikaios may be a title: "the Righteous One", as Peter calls Jesus in Acts.
b: The Greek Iēsoun Christon dikaion can be read "Jesus Christ, who is righteous" or "Jesus Christ, the Righteous One". Peter says to the crowd in the Temple, "The Holy and Righteous One you disowned" (Acts 3:14), and Isaiah's servant is "the righteous one" who "will carry their guilt" (Isaiah 53:11). Either way the point is the same: the one who pleads for sinners is not a sinner himself (3:5), which is why his plea is heard.

p: Hilasmos is a temple word: the means by which sin is covered and God's anger turned away.
b: Hilasmos comes only here and at 4:10 in the New Testament. The Greek Old Testament uses it for atonement: "the Day of Atonement" (Leviticus 25:9, hēmera tou hilasmou), the ram "to make atonement" (Numbers 5:8), and Psalm 130:4, "Yet forgiveness is found with you", where the Greek has hilasmos. Readers differ: (1) propitiation, turning aside God's anger (KJV "propitiation"); (2) expiation, wiping out sin (the English Catholic Catechism quotes 4:10 as "the expiation for our sins", paragraph 604); (3) both, since in the Bible sin removed is wrath removed. Paul uses a related word, hilastērion: "God put him forward as the place of atonement" (Romans 3:25).

a: it is for the whole world
p: Does "the whole world" mean every person, or believers everywhere? The churches answer differently.
b: Three readings: (1) every human being: Christ's sacrifice is for all, though not all receive it (the Remonstrants of 1610 quoted this verse in their second article; the General Baptists' Standard Confession of 1660 quoted it too; the Lutheran Formula of Concord cites it for the universal promise of the gospel; Wesley: "Just as wide as sin extends, the propitiation extends also"); (2) people of every nation, not only the writer's circle or only Jews: Calvin, who agreed that Christ "suffered sufficiently for the whole world", said the formula did not fit this verse, and that it "does not include the reprobate, but designates those who should believe"; (3) a sacrifice sufficient for all, effective for the chosen (the Canons of Dort). The word kosmos elsewhere in the letter means the world set against God (2:15-17; 5:19). See the card on the chapter page.

t: The tests: "Here is how we know"
p: The letter gives tests by which readers can know where they stand: obedience, love and right belief.
b: "By this we know" (en toutō ginōskomen) and its variants come again and again (2:3, 5, 18; 3:16, 19, 24; 4:2, 6, 13; 5:2). The verb "know" (ginōskō) comes 25 times in the letter. Many readers find three tests running through it: keeping God's commands, loving the brothers, and confessing Jesus as the Messiah come in the flesh. Readers differ on their purpose: tests that unmask the opponents' claims to know God; tests by which believers examine themselves; or, as the letter says at the end, a way to give assurance: "so that you will know that you have eternal life" (5:13).

p: The words are Jesus' own in the Gospel: love shows in keeping his commands.
b: "If you love me, you will keep the commands I give" (John 14:15). "Keep" (tēreō) means to watch over, guard, hold on to. In 1 John the commands are not a long list: they come down to one, "we are to believe the name of his Son Jesus Christ, and to love each other" (3:23). Jewish readers would hear the Torah's language of keeping God's commandments (Deuteronomy 6:17), now centered on the commands of Jesus.

t: Love for God, or God's love?
p: "The love of God" can mean our love for God, God's love for us, or love of God's kind.
b: The Greek genitive hē agapē tou theou is open. It can mean (1) the love people have for God (as clearly in 5:3, "Loving God means this: keeping his commands"); (2) the love God has for us, which reaches its goal in a life of obedience; or (3) the kind of love that comes from God and is like his. The Plain keeps "the love of God" so that all three stay possible. On "made complete" see 4:12.
orig: ἡ ἀγάπη τοῦ θεοῦ (hē agapē tou theou)

p: Menō, "remain, stay, live", is the letter's favorite verb: it comes 24 times.
b: Menō means to stay where one is, to last, to live somewhere. Older English Bibles say "abide". The site follows the Gospel of John, where Jesus says, "Remain in me, and I in you" (John 15:4). In 1 John believers remain in God and God in them (3:24; 4:13, 16), the word remains in them (2:14), the anointing remains (2:27), God's seed remains (3:9), and those who left "would have remained" if they had belonged (2:19). The word tells the readers: do not move; stay with what you heard from the beginning (2:24).

p: 1 John calls Jesus ekeinos, "that one", without naming him, six times.
b: The letter says ekeinos, "that one", for Jesus in 2:6; 3:3, 5, 7, 16 and 4:17, as a well-known person needs no name. Most English Bibles write "Jesus" or "he". The Plain keeps "that one" so the reader can see the habit. The demand is simple and large: whoever claims to live in him must live as he lived, and the letter will say what that means: "that one laid down his life for our sake" (3:16).

t: An old command and a new one
p: The command to love is old (Leviticus 19:18) and new (John 13:34) at the same time.
b: It is old because the readers have had it "from the beginning" of their life as believers, and because the Torah already says, "You are to love your neighbor as yourself" (Leviticus 19:18). It is new because Jesus gave it new: "I am giving you a new command: that you love each other. In the same way that I loved you, you too are to love each other" (John 13:34). The newness is the measure, "as I loved you", and the new age in which it is lived (2:8). 2 John 5 says the same in nearly the same words.

p: The new age has begun: the light John's Gospel spoke of is already shining.
b: The Gospel says, "The real light, which shines on every person, was on its way into the world" (John 1:9). The letter says that light "already shines", and the darkness "is passing away". This is the language of the end of the age (compare Romans 13:12): the age to come has broken into the present, though the old age has not yet gone (2:17). The command to love is "new" because it belongs to that new day. Alēthinos means real, genuine, as against a copy or a fake; the site renders it "real" as the Gospel does.
orig: τὸ φῶς τὸ ἀληθινὸν ἤδη φαίνει (to phōs to alēthinon ēdē phainei)

p: In 1 John a "brother" is a fellow believer, man or woman. Who counts as one is debated.
b: Adelphos is "brother"; the plural takes in the whole family, women and men, and the site keeps "brother" and "brothers" in the Plain, as Acts and Romans do, with the gloss "brother or sister". The letter uses the word 15 times, almost always of a fellow member of the church. Readers differ on how far it reaches: (1) only fellow believers, since the letter is about a divided church; (2) every neighbor, since the letter grounds love in God, who loved "the world" (4:9-14), and since Cain and Abel (3:12) were brothers by birth. Jesus' parable of the Samaritan answered the question "Who is my neighbor?" (Luke 10:29-37).

a: nothing in him to trip over
p: Skandalon is a trap or a stone to trip on. Does the one who loves not stumble, or not trip others?
b: The Greek skandalon en autō ouk estin can mean that the one who loves has nothing in his own path to trip him (he sees where he goes, unlike the hater, 2:11), or that there is nothing in him that would make others stumble. The Greek of Psalm 119:165 (118:165 in the Septuagint) uses the same words. Of those who love God's law it says, "there is no stumbling block for them" (Psalm 119:165), where the Greek is ouk estin autois skandalon. That parallel favors the first reading.

a: He has no idea where he is headed
p: The words echo Jesus' warning in John's Gospel about walking without the light.
b: Jesus says in the Gospel, "Keep walking while you have the light, so that the darkness does not take hold of you. Someone walking in the dark has no idea where he is headed" (John 12:35). The letter applies it to hatred: hating a brother is not a small fault in an otherwise enlightened life; it is the darkness itself, and it blinds. Isaiah 6:10 and John 12:40 speak of eyes blinded as well.

a: because your sins have been forgiven
p: The six lines of 2:12-14 each give a reason; the Greek hoti could also mean "that".
b: Each of the six lines in 2:12-14 has hoti, which can mean "because" (the writer writes because they are forgiven, know God and have won the victory) or "that" (he writes to tell them that they are forgiven). Most translations take "because": the letter's warnings are written to people already forgiven, not to frighten outsiders. "For the sake of his name" recalls Israel's prayer, "pardon my guilt; it is huge" (Psalm 25:11), a prayer made "because of your name".

a: Fathers, I am writing to you
p: Three groups addressed twice, once with "I am writing" and once with "I have written". Who are they?
b: The lines in 2:12-14 speak to "little children" (or "children"), "fathers" and "young men", first with "I am writing" and then with "I have written". Readers take the groups as (1) real age groups in the church; (2) stages of faith: new believers, mature ones, those in the struggle; or (3) everyone, as "little children" (the letter's name for all its readers, 2:1), and then two groups within them, older and younger. The change of tense has been read as a different letter written earlier, as the Gospel of John, as the first part of this letter, or simply as a Greek letter-writer's "I have written" for the letter in hand.

a: the one who is from the beginning
p: The one known by the "fathers" may be the Father or the Son.
b: "The one who is from the beginning" (ton ap' archēs) could be God the Father, who is also named in the last line of 2:13, or Christ, the life "that was with the Father" (1:1-2). The letter's opening uses "from the beginning" of what the eyewitnesses saw and touched, which favors Christ. The fathers' knowledge is long and settled; that is why the line is repeated without change in 2:14.

p: Ho ponēros, "the evil one", is the devil, as in the Lord's Prayer and in Jesus' prayer in John 17.
b: In the Lord's Prayer Jesus teaches, "rescue us from the evil one" (Matthew 6:13), and he prays in the Gospel, "I am asking you to keep them safe from the evil one" (John 17:15). 1 John uses the title five times (2:13, 14; 3:12; 5:18, 19) and also "the devil" (3:8, 10). The young men "have won the victory" over him already, through the word of God that remains in them (2:14), the same verb as Jesus' "I have won the victory over the world" (John 16:33).

p: God loved the world (John 3:16), yet believers must not love it. The word has two senses.
b: Kosmos comes 23 times in 1 John. Sometimes it is the human race God loves and saves: the Son is "the Savior of the world" (4:14), and "For this is how God loved the world: he gave his only Son" (John 3:16). Here it is human life organized without God and against him, which "lies in the evil one's hands" (5:19). To love that world is to want what it wants (2:16). The letter is not telling readers to despise creation or people, but to refuse a way of life that is passing away (2:17).
orig: μὴ ἀγαπᾶτε τὸν κόσμον (mē agapate ton kosmon)

a: the craving of the flesh, the craving of the eyes
p: The list has been read against Eve in the garden and against Jesus' testing in the wilderness.
b: Epithymia is strong desire, craving. "The flesh" (sarx) is human nature in its weakness and its appetites, not the body as evil. Many readers have compared the three items with the tree in Eden: "The woman saw that the tree was good to eat, that it was a delight to the eyes, and that the tree was attractive for making a person wise" (Genesis 3:6). Others compare the three tests of Jesus (Matthew 4:1-11; Luke 4:1-13). Whether or not the writer meant either, the list covers appetite, envy and pride.
orig: ἡ ἐπιθυμία τῆς σαρκός (hē epithymia tēs sarkos)

a: the bragging about what one has
p: Bios here is not "life" in general but one's living: money, goods, status.
b: The KJV's "the pride of life" is famous, but bios here means livelihood, property, the means of living, not the life God gives (zōē). Alazoneia is the swagger of a boaster. The phrase points at showing off wealth and position. The same word bios returns in 3:17: "if someone has enough to live on in this world, and sees his brother in need". The letter sets the two side by side: what one has is for one's brother, not for display.
orig: ἡ ἀλαζονεία τοῦ βίου (hē alazoneia tou biou)

p: The phrase is found only here in the New Testament. What "hour" did the writer mean?
b: Readers take "the last hour" as (1) the short time before Christ's return, which the writer believed was near (2:28); (2) the whole age between Jesus' first and second coming, which the New Testament often calls "the last days" (Acts 2:17; Hebrews 1:2); or (3) an hour of crisis for this church, in which the split showed what side each person was on. The writer's evidence is not a sign in the sky but people: the coming of "many antichrists". In John's Gospel "the hour" is Jesus' death and glory (John 12:23).

p: The word is found only in John's letters, where it names many false teachers already present.
b: "Antichrist" occurs only in 1 John 2:18, 22; 4:3 and 2 John 7. Anti can mean "against" or "in place of": one who opposes Christ, or a false Christ. The readers "heard" that one was coming, perhaps from Jesus' warnings (Mark 13:22) or from teaching like Paul's on "the man of lawlessness" (2 Thessalonians 2:3). The letter's surprise is that "many antichrists" are already here, the teachers who left (2:19, 22). Polycarp writes in the same way: "For whosoever does not confess that Jesus Christ has come in the flesh, is antichrist" (Philippians 7). The Plain writes it lower case because the letter uses it of a kind of person, not as a name.

a: They went out from among us
p: A group had left the church. The letter is written to those who stayed.
b: This verse is the clearest window on why the letter was written: a group "went out", most likely over who Jesus is (2:22; 4:2-3), and perhaps they took their teaching to other churches (4:1; 2 John 7, 10). Irenaeus, about AD 180, quotes this verse with 2:18-22 against the teachers of his own day. Raymond Brown and others built a history of the "Johannine community" on such verses; others now doubt that we can know so much (Bauckham, Reinhartz, Méndez). Christians differ on what the verse says about salvation: some read "they were never really from us" as proof that true believers do not finally fall away; others read it only as the history of one split.

a: none of them are from us
p: The Greek puts "not" before "all". Here that means "none of them", not "some of them".
b: Word for word the Greek says "that not are all from us" (ouk eisin pantes ex hēmōn). The KJV kept the order, "they were not all of us", which can sound as if some of them were. In Greek of this kind "not ... all" can mean "none": Paul writes "No flesh will be justified in his sight" (Romans 3:20), where the Greek is literally "not ... all flesh". The verse itself requires that sense, since it has just said that they "were never really from us". The BSB and the WEB also render it "none of them".
orig: οὐκ εἰσὶν πάντες ἐξ ἡμῶν (ouk eisin pantes ex hēmōn)

p: Chrisma is the oil itself. The readers are anointed, against the anti-anointed (anti-christoi).
b: Chrisma, the anointing oil, belongs to the same family as Christos, "Anointed One". The word play is plain in Greek: the antichrists have left, but you have the chrism. Wesley noted it: "A chrism; perhaps so termed in opposition to the name of antichrist". What is it? (1) The Holy Spirit, given to all believers (3:24; 4:13; compare Isaiah 61:1, Acts 10:38); (2) the word of the gospel they heard from the beginning (2:24); (3) both: the word made alive by the Spirit. In the Orthodox Church the anointing after baptism is called chrismation, "The Seal and Gift of the Holy Spirit", and Kallistos Ware cites this verse for it.

p: The anointing comes from "the Holy One": Christ, or God the Father.
b: "The Holy One" is a title of God throughout the Old Testament ("the Holy One of Israel" in Isaiah). In John's Gospel Peter calls Jesus "God's Holy One" (John 6:69), and Jesus says he will send the Spirit (John 15:26; John 16:7). So the giver is probably Christ, though God the Father gives the Spirit too (John 14:16). 2:27 says the anointing came "from him", again without naming him.

a: denies that Jesus is the Messiah
p: Denying that Jesus is the Messiah may mean a Jewish denial, or a teaching that split Jesus from the Christ.
b: Three views. (1) A denial that Jesus is the Jewish Messiah, by people who had left the church for the synagogue or held back from confessing him, as in John's Gospel (John 9:22). (2) The teaching that the man Jesus and the heavenly Christ were two: Irenaeus reports that Cerinthus taught that "after his baptism, Christ descended upon him in the form of a dove" and that "at last Christ departed from Jesus, and that then Jesus suffered and rose again, while Christ remained impassible" (Against Heresies 1.26.1). (3) Docetism, the claim that Christ only seemed to have a body (4:2). Views (2) and (3) explain the letter's stress on the flesh (4:2-3) and on the blood (5:6).

a: what you heard from the beginning must remain in you
p: The cure for new teaching is the old message: stay with what you first heard.
b: The opponents may have offered something new and deeper. The writer answers by pointing back: what you heard "from the beginning" (1:1; 2:7; 3:11). If it remains in you, you remain in the Son and the Father. 2 John 9 makes the same point against anyone who "goes ahead" and does not remain in the teaching of Christ. The idea is not that believers cannot grow, but that growth stays rooted in the first message about Jesus.

a: you do not need anyone to teach you
p: The writer is teaching even as he says this. What does he mean?
b: The words echo the new covenant promise: no one will need to teach his neighbor to know the LORD, "Because they will all know me, from the smallest of them to the greatest" (Jeremiah 31:34). Jesus promised that the Advocate "will teach you everything" (John 14:26). The point is that the readers do not need the opponents' new teaching: the Spirit who taught them the gospel is enough. It is not a rejection of teachers, since the writer is one. Some readers take it as a promise of the Spirit's direct guidance for every believer; others answer that it is about the gospel already received, not private revelation.

p: Menete can mean "you remain" or "remain!". The Plain takes the command, as 2:28 does.
b: The Greek form menete is the same for "you remain" and "remain!". It may close 2:27 as a promise ("you do remain in him") or as a call ("remain in him"). The next verse begins "So now ... remain in him" with the same word, which suggests the call. The Byzantine text and the KJV have the future, "ye shall abide in him".

p: The only place in John's writings with parousia, Christ's royal "coming".
b: Ean is "if" or "whenever"; the writer is not doubting the return but leaving its time open. Parousia, "coming", was the word for the arrival of a king or governor on a visit. Paul uses it often (1 Thessalonians 4:15; 1 Corinthians 15:23); this is its only use in John's Gospel and letters. The Byzantine text and the KJV read "when he shall appear".
orig: ἐν τῇ παρουσίᾳ αὐτοῦ (en tē parousia autou)

p: Parrēsia, freedom of speech, was a citizen's right to speak openly. Here it is before God.
b: Parrēsia was a citizen's right to speak his mind in the assembly, and the openness of a friend. The site renders it "freedom of speech" or "speak freely" in Acts. 1 John uses it four times: freedom to speak at Christ's coming (2:28), before God in prayer (3:21; 5:14), and on the day of judgment (4:17). The opposite is shame: to be "shamed away from him", to shrink back like a guilty servant before his returning master.

p: The first of ten places in 1 John that speak of being born from God.
b: "Born from God" (ek tou theou gegennētai) is a key idea of the letter (2:29; 3:9 twice; 4:7; 5:1 three times, 4, 18 twice). The Gospel says of those who receive Jesus, "Their birth came not from blood, not from fleshly desire, not from a man's decision, but from God" (John 1:13), and Jesus tells Nicodemus that one must be "born from above" (John 3:3). In the letter the birth shows in the family likeness: the child does what the Father does, righteousness and love.

p: Potapēn asks "of what country?": a love from somewhere else, unlike any other.
b: Potapos first meant "from what country?" and came to mean "of what sort?", usually with wonder: what amazing kind of love. The love is not only felt but "given" (dedōken), and the gift is a new standing: to be called God's children. The world's failure to recognize believers is no surprise, because it did not recognize Jesus either (John 1:10; John 15:18).

p: John calls believers tekna, "children", and keeps "Son" (huios) for Jesus alone.
b: The Gospel says that to those who received him Jesus "gave the authority to become God's children: to those who believe in his name" (John 1:12). John's writings call believers tekna theou, "children of God", born from him (2:29; 3:9), and keep huios, "Son", for Jesus alone. Paul uses "sons" and the picture of adoption (Romans 8:14-17; Galatians 4:5); John uses the picture of birth. Both say believers share the family life of God.

p: Catholics read the verse of the vision of God, the Orthodox of theosis; others of the risen body.
b: "He" may be Christ, whose appearing the letter awaits (2:28), or God the Father. Readers draw out the promise in different ways. The Catholic Catechism cites the verse for the vision of God in heaven: the blessed "see him as he is", face to face (paragraphs 163, 1023). An Orthodox article published for the Antiochian archdiocese cites it for theosis, "real union with God". Wesley wrote that it "will raise the children of God to be, in a manner, as God himself". Many Protestants stress the raised body made like Christ's (Philippians 3:21). All agree that the full likeness is still future.

a: we will see him just as he is
p: Jesus promised that the pure in heart will see God; Paul says that now we see only a riddle.
b: "Blessed are those whose hearts are pure, because they will see God" (Matthew 5:8). Paul: "For now we look through a mirror, and what we see is a riddle. But then we will see face to face" (1 Corinthians 13:12). Revelation: "They will see his face" (Revelation 22:4). The Old Testament warned that no one could see God and live (Exodus 33:20), and 1 John itself says that "No one has ever gazed at God" (4:12). The promise is that what is impossible now will be given then, and that the sight will change the one who sees.

p: Hagnizō was the word for the purification Jews did before a festival.
b: In the Gospel, before the last Passover, "Many people from the countryside went up to Jerusalem ahead of the Passover to make themselves pure" (John 11:55): the same verb, hagnizō. The Greek Old Testament uses it for the Levites' and the Nazirites' cleansing (Numbers 8:21; Numbers 6:3). The letter turns it inward and forward: those who hope to see the Lord prepare for that meeting the way a pilgrim prepares for a feast, by becoming pure "just as that one is pure".

p: The KJV's "sin is the transgression of the law" narrows it. Anomia is lawlessness, rebellion.
b: Anomia literally means "being without law". The KJV's "sin is the transgression of the law" makes it a breach of a rule. But in the New Testament anomia is often the rebellion of the last days: "the man of lawlessness" (2 Thessalonians 2:3) and the growth of lawlessness Jesus foretold (Matthew 24:12). Read that way, the verse says that sin is not a small thing: it takes the side of the end-time rebel, the antichrist (2:18). Others read it simply: every sin is a refusal of God's law.
orig: ἡ ἁμαρτία ἐστὶν ἡ ἀνομία (hē hamartia estin hē anomia)

t: He appeared to take sins away
p: The words recall John the Baptist: "the one who takes the world's sin away".
b: In the Gospel John the Baptist calls Jesus "the Lamb of God" and "the one who takes the world's sin away" (John 1:29), with the same verb airō, to lift up and carry off. The letter adds "in him there is no sin": the one who takes sin away has none of his own, which is why he can be the "atoning sacrifice" (2:2) and the Advocate who is "righteous" (2:1). Compare John 8:46 and 2 Corinthians 5:21.
r: John 1:29; Isaiah 53:4-12; John 8:46; 2 Corinthians 5:21; Hebrews 4:15; 1 Peter 2:22

p: The letter says the believer "does not sin" (3:6, 9) after saying all of us sin (1:8-10). Readings.
b: The Greek is plain: ouch hamartanei, "does not sin"; 3:9 adds "cannot sin". Many modern Bibles write "keep on sinning", because the present tense can describe a habit. But the present tense alone does not settle it: 1:8 and 5:16 use present tenses of sin in believers. Readings: (1) habitual sin: a believer may sin but does not live in sin; (2) a particular sin, the "sin headed toward death" (5:16) or the end-time "lawlessness" (3:4); (3) the believer's new nature, what the child of God is, while 1:8 describes what he still does (Calvin: "the Spirit of God restrains the lusting of sin"); (4) Wesley: "sinneth not - While he so abideth", the basis of his teaching on Christian perfection. The Plain keeps the Greek's bluntness. See the deep dive on the chapter page.

a: to undo the works of the devil
p: Lyō means to untie, break up, undo. The devil's works began "from the beginning".
b: "From the beginning" here means from the start of the world's story. Jesus says of the devil in the Gospel, "From the start he was a killer of people" (John 8:44): the same Greek ap' archēs. The Son appeared to "undo" (lysē) the devil's works, the verb for untying a knot or breaking down a building (John 2:19). Readers have seen in it the first promise of Genesis 3:15, that the woman's offspring would crush the serpent. Hebrews 2:14 says the same in other words.
orig: ἵνα λύσῃ τὰ ἔργα τοῦ διαβόλου (hina lysē ta erga tou diabolou)

p: Sperma may be God's nature, his Spirit, his word, or his offspring.
b: Sperma means seed or offspring. Readings: (1) God's own life or nature planted in the believer at the new birth, the most common view; (2) the Holy Spirit (3:24); (3) the word of God, as Peter says: "The seed it came from was not one that decays but one that cannot decay: God's word, which is alive and remains" (1 Peter 1:23), and Jesus: "The seed is the word of God" (Luke 8:11); (4) God's "seed" as his children, so that "his offspring remain in him", that is, in God. Wesley wrote, "the divine seed of loving faith abideth in him".

a: God's children and the devil's children
p: A Jewish way of speaking. The letter applies it to members of the church, not to Jews.
b: The Dead Sea Scrolls divide humanity in the same way: "All the children of righteousness are ruled by the Prince of Light", and "all the children of falsehood are ruled by the Angel of Darkness" (Community Rule, column 3, lines 19-21, in Vermes's translation). In John's Gospel Jesus says to some who argued with him, "You come from your father, the devil" (John 8:44), words later used against the Jewish people as a whole, with terrible results. In 1 John the line is drawn inside the church: the test is whether a person does righteousness and loves his brother. No people or nation is meant.

p: Some Jewish traditions made Cain the offspring of an angel or of Sammael. The letter says he was "from the evil one".
b: Genesis tells it simply: "Cain turned on Abel his brother and killed him" (Genesis 4:8). Later Jewish retellings darkened Cain. The Targum Pseudo-Jonathan on Genesis 4:1 says that Eve "had desired the Angel" and calls the child "the Angel of the Lord" (Etheridge's translation), and Pirkei de-Rabbi Eliezer (chapter 21) says Sammael, "riding on the serpent", came to Eve and she conceived Cain. 1 John says only that Cain was "from the evil one", the way it speaks of the devil's children (3:8, 10), by what he did. Jude also warns of those who "have walked the road Cain walked" (Jude 1:11).

p: Sphazō is the butcher's and the priest's word: to cut the throat, as of a sacrifice.
b: Genesis says only that Cain "killed" Abel. 1 John uses sphazō, "slaughter", the word for killing a sacrificial animal, and the word Revelation uses of the Lamb, who "looked as though he had been slaughtered" (Revelation 5:6). The choice may hint at the irony of Genesis 4: Cain the offerer becomes a killer, and Abel, who brought the better offering, becomes the victim. The reason given is moral: Cain's deeds were evil, Abel's righteous.

a: we have moved out of death and into life
p: The words are Jesus' own in John 5:24, nearly letter for letter in Greek.
b: Jesus says in the Gospel that anyone who listens to his word and believes "has eternal life. He is not coming into judgment. He has already moved out of death and into life" (John 5:24). The Greek verb metabainō and the phrase are the same here. The Gospel's test is belief; the letter's is love for the brothers. The two belong together (3:23). The new life is present already, not only after death.

p: Like Jesus in the Sermon on the Mount, the letter traces murder back to hatred.
b: Anthrōpoktonos, "man-killer", is used in the New Testament only here and of the devil: "From the start he was a killer of people" (John 8:44). Jesus taught that anger is already liable to judgment: "But I myself tell you: everyone who is angry with his brother must stand trial" (Matthew 5:22). The Torah already forbids hating one's brother in the heart (Leviticus 19:17). The letter does not mean that a hater is legally a murderer, but that hate belongs to the same family as Cain's act and the devil's work.

a: that one laid down his life for our sake
p: The phrase is the Good Shepherd's in John 10, and it becomes the pattern for every believer.
b: "I am the good shepherd. The good shepherd lays down his own life for the sheep" (John 10:11). "There is no greater love anyone can have than this: to lay down his life for the sake of his friends" (John 15:13). The letter defines love not by a feeling but by this act, and then draws the line straight to the reader: we are "bound" (opheilomen, "owe it") to do the same. The next verse brings it down to everyday life: sharing what one has.

p: The Torah forbids hardening one's heart against a brother in need. The letter calls it a loss of God's love.
b: The Greek says he shuts his splanchna, his "insides", the seat of feeling in Greek and Hebrew thought. The Torah says: "If so, do not harden your heart or close your hand against your brother in need" (Deuteronomy 15:7). The letter makes the test practical: "enough to live on" is the same word bios as "what one has" in 2:16. James asks the same question about faith without deeds (James 2:15-16).
orig: κλείσῃ τὰ σπλάγχνα αὐτοῦ (kleisē ta splanchna autou)

a: God is greater than our heart
p: "God is greater than our heart" can comfort a troubled conscience, or warn a careless one.
b: The Greek of 3:19-20 is hard to construe, and the sense can go two ways. (1) Comfort: when our conscience accuses us, God, who knows everything, knows our love and his own mercy better than our fearful heart does, and so our heart can be calmed "before him". (2) Warning: if even our own heart condemns us, how much more God, who knows all. The context favors the comfort: 3:19 speaks of calming the heart, and 3:21 of freedom before God. The Catholic Catechism quotes the words in its teaching on God's mercy (paragraph 208).

a: we receive from him anything we ask for
p: The promise repeats Jesus' words at the Last Supper, with a condition the letter spells out later.
b: Jesus says, "Anything you ask for in my name, I will do it" (John 14:13), and "Keep asking and you will receive, so that your joy will be filled up" (John 16:24). The letter links answered prayer to obedience, not as payment but as the life of a child who wants what the Father wants. 5:14 states the condition: "if we ask anything in line with his will, he hears us".

a: we are to believe the name of his Son Jesus Christ
p: "His command" is singular: believing and loving are one command, not two.
b: The letter's many "commands" come down to one ("His command is this") with two sides: to believe and to love. "Believe the name" (pisteusōmen tō onomati, without "in") means to trust what the name says Jesus is: the Son, the Messiah. The first time the letter uses "believe", it joins it at once to love. In the Gospel Jesus says, "Here is the work of God: that you believe in the one that he sent" (John 6:29), and "Here is my command: that you love each other just as I loved you" (John 15:12).

a: from the Spirit he has given us
p: The first mention of the Spirit in the letter: the sign that God remains in us.
b: Here the Spirit is named for the first time, as the evidence that God remains in believers; 4:13 repeats it. The Spirit is not a private experience set against the letter's other tests, for the next verses at once say to test the spirits by what they confess (4:1-3). The Gospel's promise lies behind it: "he remains beside you, and he will be in you" (John 14:17).

a: Put the spirits to the test
p: Early churches had prophets who spoke by a spirit. The letter gives a test: what they confess about Jesus.
b: Prophecy was part of church life (1 Corinthians 12:10, "telling spirits apart"; 1 Thessalonians 5:21, "put everything to the test"). Behind every prophet, the letter says, stands a spirit, either God's or another. The Torah gave Israel tests: a prophet whose word does not come true, or who leads to other gods, is not from the LORD (Deuteronomy 13:1-5; Deuteronomy 18:21-22). The letter's test is about Jesus: does the spirit confess him as having come in the flesh (4:2)? Jesus too warned that "false messiahs and false prophets will rise up" (Mark 13:22).
r: Deuteronomy 13:1-5; Deuteronomy 18:21-22; Mark 13:22; 1 Corinthians 12:10; 1 Thessalonians 5:20-21; Revelation 2:2

a: as having come in the flesh
t: Come in the flesh: docetism and Cerinthus
p: On the usual reading, the test aims at teachers who denied that the Christ truly became human, or who split Jesus from the Christ.
b: The perfect participle elēlythota says he came and still is the one who came in the flesh. Two early teachings deny it. Docetism (from Greek dokein, "to seem") said Christ only seemed to have a body. Cerinthus, Irenaeus reports, taught that Christ came on Jesus at his baptism and left before the passion (Against Heresies 1.26.1). Irenaeus also tells a story from Polycarp that John fled a bath-house at Ephesus because "Cerinthus, the enemy of the truth, is within" (Against Heresies 3.3.4). The Gospel's answer is the same: "And the Word became flesh and pitched his tent among us" (John 1:14). Terry Griffith reads the phrase with no such target: "Jesus, Messiah come in the flesh", that is, the promised Messiah has come into the world and he is Jesus, a restatement of 2:22. 2 John 7 says "coming in the flesh" with a present participle.

a: This is what belongs to the antichrist
p: The Greek says only "the thing of the antichrist". Most English Bibles add "spirit".
b: The Greek to tou antichristou is neuter and has no noun: "that which is of the antichrist". English Bibles usually supply "the spirit of the antichrist", which fits the context (spirits are being tested), but the Greek may mean something wider: the activity, the power or the movement of the antichrist. The point is the same: the opponents' teaching is the antichrist that the readers were told to expect, already at work.

a: greater is the one in you than the one in the world
t: Greater is the one in you
p: The one in believers is God (or his Spirit); the one in the world is the devil, "this world's ruler".
b: The one "in you" is God, or the Spirit he has given (3:24; 4:13); the one "in the world" is the evil one (5:19). In the Gospel Jesus calls him "this world's ruler" and says, "About judgment: this world's ruler has already been judged" (John 16:11). The readers have "won the victory" over the false prophets not by their own strength but because the one who lives in them is stronger.

a: the Spirit of truth and the spirit that leads astray
p: The Dead Sea Scrolls speak of "the spirits of truth and falsehood" in very similar words.
b: In the Gospel the Holy Spirit is "the Spirit of truth" (John 14:17; John 15:26). The opposite here is to pneuma tēs planēs, "the spirit of going astray", from the same root as "lead astray" (1:8; 2:26; 3:7). The Community Rule from Qumran says God appointed for humanity "the spirits of truth and falsehood", by which people walk (Community Rule, column 3, lines 18-19, in Vermes's translation). The pairing is old Jewish language; 1 John puts Jesus at its center: the Spirit of truth confesses him.

p: The test of the spirits ends with a test of the hearers: do they listen to the apostolic "we"?
b: Jesus says in the Gospel, "The one who is from God listens to God's words" (John 8:47), and "My own sheep pay attention to my voice" (John 10:27). Here the "we" who must be heard are the bearers of the eyewitness message (1:1-3). Readers differ on how far this reaches: to the apostles and their writings, now the New Testament; to the teaching of the apostles as it is handed on in the church; or only to this writer and his circle against those who had left.

p: Not "love is God": love is what God is, and loving is how one knows him.
b: The sentence comes twice (4:8, 16). Wesley noted that God is often called holy, righteous and wise, "but not holiness, righteousness, or wisdom in the abstract", as he is here called love. The Catholic Catechism: "God's very being is love" (paragraph 221). Augustine, preaching on this letter, even turned it around, "Love is of God: Love IS God", and drew the famous rule, "Love, and do what you will" (Homilies on 1 John 7.5, 7.8), meaning that the deeds of one whose root is love will be good. The letter itself explains the love by an act, the sending of the Son (4:9-10), so it is no vague feeling.
orig: ὁ θεὸς ἀγάπη ἐστίν (ho theos agapē estin)

p: Monogenēs means "only, unique", not "only begotten" in the sense of a birth.
b: Monogenēs is used of an only child (Luke 7:12; Luke 8:42; Hebrews 11:17 of Isaac). The KJV's "only begotten" connects the second half of the word with the verb "beget"; others connect it with genos, "kind", and so read "only, unique". The site renders it as the Gospel does: "For this is how God loved the world: he gave his only Son, so that everyone who believes in him would not be lost but would have eternal life" (John 3:16). 1 John 4:9 uses the same word for "only", with a different verb: the Gospel says God "gave" (edōken) his Son, the letter that he "has sent" (apestalken) him, a fact already accomplished.
orig: τὸν υἱὸν αὐτοῦ τὸν μονογενῆ (ton huion autou ton monogenē)

a: It is not that we have loved God
p: The letter's definition of love: not ours for God, but God's for us, shown in the Son's death.
b: "Love is in this": the letter does not start with human love and rise to God. It starts with God's act, the sending of the Son as "the atoning sacrifice where our sins are concerned" (see 2:2). The Catholic Catechism quotes the verse in its English as "to be the expiation for our sins" (paragraph 604), which shows how translators differ on hilasmos. 4:19 draws the conclusion: "We love because he loved us first."

a: if that is how God loved us
p: A scrap of papyrus from Egypt, from the 200s, holds parts of 4:11-17.
b: Among the earliest surviving copies of 1 John is Papyrus 9 (Oxyrhynchus papyrus 402), one leaf found at Oxyrhynchus in Egypt and now at Harvard. It is dated by its handwriting to the 200s and holds 4:11-12 and 4:14-17. Its writing is crude and careless, with some spellings that cannot be made out as words, so it is evidence that the letter was being read in ordinary hands, not a polished copy. The great codices of the 300s and 400s (Vaticanus, Sinaiticus, Alexandrinus) contain the whole letter.

a: No one has ever gazed at God
p: The Gospel says the same, then points to the Son. The letter points to love among believers.
b: The Gospel says, "Nobody has ever seen God. It is the only one, God, the one in the Father's embrace, who has made him known" (John 1:18), and the Torah, "no human being can see me and stay alive" (Exodus 33:20). The letter uses the verb of 1:1, theaomai, "gaze at". Its answer is surprising: the unseen God becomes present where believers love each other. God "remains in us" and his love reaches its goal in us. On "made complete" (teteleiōmenē), see 4:17-18.

p: The title is found only twice in the New Testament: here, and from the Samaritans in John 4.
b: After Jesus stayed two days in their town, the Samaritans said, "We have heard for ourselves, and we know that he is truly the Savior of the world" (John 4:42). "Savior" (sōtēr) was also a title claimed by Roman emperors. "We ourselves have gazed at this" returns to the eyewitness "we" of 1:1-3. The world that "lies in the evil one's hands" (5:19) is also the world the Father sent the Son to save (2:2; John 3:17).

p: "Come to know" and "believed" stand together, as in Peter's confession in John 6:69.
b: Both verbs are perfects: a knowing and a believing that started in the past and continue. The Gospel joins them the same way in Peter's words: "We for our part have believed, and we have come to know, that you are God's Holy One" (John 6:69). "Among us" (en hēmin) can also be read "in us" or "for us": the love God has shown in the community, or toward it.

p: "As that one is, so are we in this world": a hard phrase. Who is like whom, and how?
b: The letter expects a final judgment, which it names only here. Believers can face it with "freedom to speak" (see 2:28). The reason is the obscure clause "as that one is, so are we in this world". Readings: (1) we are in this world what Christ is, loved by the Father, and so we need not fear; (2) we live in the world as he lived, in love (2:6); (3) as Christ now stands before the Father, so we too will stand, because we are in him. All agree that love completed in us is the ground for confidence, not our own record.

p: The KJV's "perfect love casteth out fear". Teleios is love that has reached its goal.
b: Teleia agapē is love made complete (the verb teleioō comes in 2:5; 4:12, 17, 18); the site renders the word family "complete", as John 17:23 does, but the KJV's "perfect love" is the famous form. The fear is the fear of "punishment" (kolasis, as in Matthew 25:46, "eternal punishment"), the fear of a slave before a master. This is not the "fear of the LORD" that "is where knowledge begins" (Proverbs 1:7), reverence and awe. Wesley drew the line: "No slavish fear can be where love reigns." Paul: "You did not receive a spirit that makes you slaves again, to live in fear" (Romans 8:15).
orig: ἡ τελεία ἀγάπη ἔξω βάλλει τὸν φόβον (hē teleia agapē exō ballei ton phobon)

p: Love for the unseen God is tested by love for the brother one can see.
b: The argument runs from the easier to the harder: if a person cannot love the brother in front of him, his claim to love God, whom no one has seen (4:12), is empty. The writer calls it a lie. Jesus joins the two great commands in the Gospels: love God, and "You are to love your neighbor as yourself" (Mark 12:31). Some readers take the verse as saying that love of neighbor is the way to love God; others, that it is the proof of it.

t: Believing that Jesus is the Messiah
p: The confession the opponents denied (2:22) is the mark of the one born from God.
b: The Gospel ends its main story with the same words: "These have been written down so that you may believe that Jesus is the Messiah, the Son of God, and so that as you believe, you will have life in his name" (John 20:31). The letter ties that belief to the new birth: whoever believes it "has been born from God" (perfect tense: the birth has already happened). It is the positive side of 2:22, where the liar denies it.

t: Love the Father, love his children
p: A family rule: if you love a parent, you love the parent's children too.
b: Ton gennēsanta is "the one who fathered" and ton gegennēmenon "the one fathered". The sentence is a general truth of family life, applied to God: love for God includes love for everyone he has fathered. Some ancient readers took "the one born from him" as Christ, the Son; but the next verse speaks of "God's children" in the plural, which favors the believers.

p: God's commands are not a crushing load: the Torah says so, and Jesus says his load is light.
b: Bareiai means heavy, burdensome. Moses says, "This command I am giving you today is not too strange or hard for you, and it is not far away" (Deuteronomy 30:11), and Jesus, "For my yoke is kind to wear, and the load I give is light" (Matthew 11:30). The reason given follows: the one born from God already has the victory (5:4). The commands are not light because they ask little (3:16 asks one's life), but because love carries them.

a: wins the victory over the world
p: Nikaō, "win the victory", recalls Jesus' "I have won the victory over the world" (John 16:33).
b: Jesus says at the Last Supper, "In the world you have hardship. But be brave: I have won the victory over the world" (John 16:33). The letter uses the same verb six times (2:13, 14; 4:4; 5:4 twice, 5). Revelation promises its rewards "to the one who wins the victory" in each of the seven letters. The victory is not future only: it "has won", a past act. "Our faith" is the only place the noun pistis appears in John's Gospel and letters; the Gospel uses the verb "believe" (98 times in this site's Greek word list) but never the noun.

a: He came not in the water only, but in the water and in the blood
p: Jesus' baptism and death? The water and blood from his side? Baptism and the Lord's Supper?
b: Readings: (1) his baptism and his death: Jesus was the Christ not only at his baptism but on the cross, against a teaching like that of Cerinthus, which Irenaeus reports, that Christ came upon Jesus at baptism and left before the passion; (2) the blood and water from his side: "right away blood and water came out" (John 19:34), with the eyewitness who "has given testimony" (John 19:35); (3) the church's sacraments, baptism and the Lord's Supper, through which the testimony goes on in the church (5:8); (4) his human birth. Many hold more than one at once. The repeated "not ... only" suggests that someone accepted the water but not the blood.

p: In the Gospel the Spirit of truth is the witness to Jesus. Here he is called "the truth" itself.
b: Jesus says, "He is the Spirit of truth, who proceeds from the Father, and he will be a witness about me" (John 15:26). The letter goes further: "the Spirit is the truth", as Jesus calls himself "the truth" (John 14:6). The Spirit testifies now, in the church, to what the water and the blood showed then.

p: The Torah required two or three witnesses. Some early Latin readers heard the Trinity in "these three are one".
b: "A matter is to stand on the word of two witnesses or on the word of three witnesses" (Deuteronomy 19:15). The Spirit, the water and the blood are the three, and eis to hen eisin, "they are toward the one thing", means they agree. Cyprian of Carthage (died 258) wrote of the Father, Son and Spirit, "And these three are one" (On the Unity of the Church 6); scholars debate whether he knew the longer text or was reading the Trinity into these words. That kind of reading probably gave rise to the added words of the Latin and the KJV: see the variant on 5:7 and the deep dive on the chapter page.

a: If we receive the testimony of people
p: The argument runs from the lesser to the greater, as Jesus argues in John 5.
b: "Testimony" (martyria) and "testify" come ten times in 5:6-11. Courts accept human witnesses; God's witness is greater. Jesus argues the same way in the Gospel: "I do not take my testimony from a human being" (John 5:34), and "The one who sent me, the Father, has testified about me himself" (John 5:37). What God's testimony is, 5:11 states: eternal life in his Son.

a: Whoever has the Son has the life
p: Life is not a thing apart from Jesus: to have him is to have it.
b: The Gospel says, "The one who believes in the Son has eternal life. The one who disobeys the Son will not see life; instead God's wrath remains on him" (John 3:36). The letter sharpens it: the life is "in his Son" (5:11), so it comes with him and not otherwise. That is why the false teaching about the Son mattered so much to the writer: a different Jesus would mean no life at all.

a: so that you will know that you have eternal life
p: The letter's stated purpose is assurance. How sure a believer can be is debated between the churches.
b: John's Gospel was written "so that you may believe" (John 20:31); the letter, so that believers "will know" they have eternal life. The verb is oida, to know as a settled fact. Christians differ on how much certainty about final salvation this gives (see the perseverance cards, such as the one at 2 Corinthians 13:5). But the letter's tests (faith, obedience, love) were written to strengthen, not to frighten, people who believe.
orig: ἵνα εἰδῆτε ὅτι ζωὴν ἔχετε αἰώνιον (hina eidēte hoti zōēn echete aiōnion)

t: Prayer in line with God's will
p: Answered prayer has a condition, the one Jesus prayed in Gethsemane.
b: The promise of 3:22 is now explained: prayer is heard when it asks "in line with his will" (kata to thelēma autou). It is the prayer Jesus taught, "May your will be done" (Matthew 6:10) and prayed (Mark 14:36). The "freedom" (parrēsia, 2:28) is a child's freedom to ask, not a power to command.

p: The Greek says only "he will give him life": God, or the one who prays?
b: The sentence changes subject without saying so: "he will ask, and he will give him life". Most read the giver as God, who answers the prayer. Others take it as the one praying, who "gives" life by his prayer, as James says the one who brings a sinner back "will save his soul from death" (James 5:20). The Plain keeps "he" both times, so the reader sees the ambiguity. Either way, praying for a brother who sins is a duty, not an option.

a: There is sin headed toward death
p: Apostasy? Denying Christ? Mortal sin? A sin punished by death? The churches read it differently.
b: Readings: (1) apostasy, the rejection of Christ by those who "went out from us" (2:19, 22): Calvin, "apostasy, by which men wholly alienate themselves from God"; Wesley, "total apostasy"; (2) mortal sin, as against venial: the Catholic Catechism finds the distinction "already evident in Scripture" and cites these verses (paragraph 1854); (3) a sin God punishes with bodily death, like Ananias (Acts 5:5) or the sick at Corinth (1 Corinthians 11:30), a reading Wesley also allows; (4) the Torah's sin with "a high hand" against sin "by mistake": "But the person who acts with a high hand ... That person will be cut off from among his people" (Numbers 15:30). Clement of Alexandria already cites these verses for "the differences of sins". See the card on the chapter page.
r: Numbers 15:27-31; Leviticus 4:2; Acts 5:1-11; 1 Corinthians 11:30; Hebrews 6:4-6; Hebrews 10:26; Mark 3:28-29

p: "The one born from God" may be Christ, keeping the believer, or the believer keeping himself.
b: The verse uses "born from God" twice, first with a perfect (ho gegennēmenos, the believer, as everywhere in the letter) and then with an aorist (ho gennētheis). If the next word is "him" (auton), the second "one born from God" is probably Christ, the Son born of the Father, who keeps the believer safe, as Jesus prays, "keep them safe from the evil one" (John 17:15). If it is "himself" (heauton), as in NA28 and the Plain, it is the believer, who guards himself as 5:21 commands. See the variant. The NET Bible, which prefers "him", takes God as the one who protects.

a: lies in the evil one's hands
p: The Greek says the whole world "lies in the evil one", as a child in someone's arms, or a body in a grave.
b: En tō ponērō keitai: the world "lies" in the evil one, helpless, in his power. The Gospel calls him "this world's ruler" (John 12:31; John 14:30). Some read tō ponērō as neuter, "in evil", but the masculine "the evil one" in 5:18 makes the person more likely. The contrast is sharp: believers are "from God", the world lies in the evil one, and yet God sent his Son as "the Savior of the world" (4:14).
orig: ἐν τῷ πονηρῷ κεῖται (en tō ponērō keitai)

p: Alēthinos means real, genuine, as against false gods and idols (5:21).
b: Ho alēthinos is "the real one", the true God as against fakes. The KJV and most Bibles say "him that is true". The site follows the Gospel, which renders the same word "real": "Eternal life is this: to know you, the only real God, and the one you sent, Jesus Christ" (John 17:3). The contrast comes in the next verse: idols. Some witnesses add "God" after the first "the one who is real" (see the variant).

a: This one is the real God and eternal life
p: "This one" may point back to Jesus Christ, just named, or to the Father, "the one who is real".
b: The pronoun houtos, "this one", most naturally points to the nearest name, "Jesus Christ": then the letter ends by calling Jesus "the real God and eternal life", as it began with "the eternal life that was with the Father" (1:2), and as the Gospel begins and ends (John 1:1; John 20:28, "My Lord and my God!"). Others point out that "the one who is real" in this verse is the Father, and that John 17:3 calls the Father "the only real God", so "this one" would be the Father. The grammar allows both, and commentators divide: Albert Barnes holds that "Christ is the immediate antecedent of the pronoun", and Terry Griffith that the referent of "the true God" is Jesus; Meyer's commentary answers that "It is only the Father of Jesus Christ that is the true God"; A. Plummer judged that it is "impossible to determine with certainty".

p: The letter ends without a farewell, on a warning about idols. Real statues, or false ideas of God?
b: Readings: (1) real idols: Ephesus and the cities of Asia were full of temples, including the great temple of Artemis and the shrines of the emperors, and Christians faced pressure to join in (Revelation 2:14, 20); (2) the false teaching itself, a false god made by the opponents' minds, opposed to "the real God" just named (5:20); (3) anything put in God's place; (4) Terry Griffith reads the warning as aimed at Jewish believers tempted to return to the synagogue, turning Judaism's own polemic against idols back on it. The Jewish background is the first commandment and the prophets' mockery of idols. "Guard" (phylaxate) is a sentry's word.
orig: φυλάξατε ἑαυτὰ ἀπὸ τῶν εἰδώλων (phylaxate heauta apo tōn eidōlōn)
